title: The Setpoint Call
primary_metric: total cost per bottle over the life of the new co-packing contract, comparing the calculus-optimal line speed (reachable only after a guarding retrofit) against the line's current rated safe-speed ceiling

options.A: The Guarding Upgrade -- fund a guarding/interlock retrofit now to legally clear Line 3 for the calculus-derived cost-minimizing speed
options.B: The Rated Cap -- hold Line 3 at its current manufacturer-rated maximum safe speed for the life of the contract, with no capital outlay

This case's actual math (a genuine product of two rate functions, one increasing and one decreasing in the process variable r) forces the product rule and, to classify the resulting critical point, concavity -- both thin (n<=2) and NOT claimed by cases/the-marginal-call, which claimed derivative/critical-point/local-minimum/power-rule/quotient-rule/find-critical-points/first-derivative-test/optimization-problem/percent-of-number from this same neighborhood. The chain rule and the tangent-line-at-a-point how-to were considered and ruled out: this case's two cost factors (a+b*r) and (1/r+d) are both differentiated directly via the sum/power rules with no composite (nested) function anywhere, so the chain rule is never genuinely forced; no deliverable asks for a tangent line's equation at a specific point (the case only needs the derivative's zero, not its value used as a slope for a line), so that how-to is not forced either. Reinforcing product rule + concavity, both still thin post-'The Alert Curve', deepens real coverage rather than manufacturing a fake new claim -- the same honest-zero pattern already established by 'The Curve's Turn' and 'The Optimal Can' (see skills/case-readiness/SKILL.md's 2026-08-17 T1-10 reinforcement carve-out).

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Marisol Feng, process engineer at Bellcross Bottling

deliverables.text: A total-cost-per-bottle function TC(r), where r is Line 3's operating speed in bottles per minute: using Appendix A's cost-rate-per-minute function CR(r) and time-per-bottle function MPU(r), combine them as TC(r) = CR(r) x MPU(r) -- showing how you built each factor before multiplying.

Using the product rule (and the power rule where a factor contains a 1/r term), differentiate TC(r) with respect to r, set TC'(r) = 0, and solve algebraically for the speed r* that minimizes cost per bottle -- showing every step of the product-rule algebra, including which terms cancel.

Using both the first derivative test and a concavity (second-derivative) check, confirm that r* is a genuine local minimum and not a local maximum. In your own words, explain what a local maximum would look like on this same cost curve, and state whether TC(r) actually has one for r > 0.

A check of r* against Appendix B's rated safe-speed ceiling: state whether the unconstrained calculus optimum is legally reachable under Line 3's current guarding, then evaluate TC(r) at both r* and the rated ceiling -- showing every calculation.

A total-cost-per-bottle comparison over the life of the new contract for both real paths: for The Guarding Upgrade, combine TC(r*) with Appendix C's retrofit cost spread evenly across Appendix C's contract volume; for The Rated Cap, use TC at the rated ceiling with no retrofit cost added. State which path has the lower true cost per bottle and by how much, in dollars and as a percent.
An original visual display (a graph of TC(r), built in Desmos or by hand, or an equivalent chart) showing cost per bottle versus line speed, with r* and the rated ceiling both labeled.

appendices.title: Line 3's Rated Speed and the Safety Standard
The Two Paths' Costs and the Contract

balance.argument_a: The Guarding Upgrade genuinely lowers the theoretical cost per bottle: TC(r*) = $0.023767/bottle at r* = 335.41 bpm, versus $0.025600/bottle at the current rated ceiling (150 bpm) -- a real, correctly-computed result of D2's product-rule minimization, 7.7% cheaper on the raw calculus alone. The flaw in stopping there is that reaching r* is not free: it requires a $44,000 guarding/interlock retrofit (MA6), which must be amortized across Appendix C's 10,000,000-bottle contract volume (MA7) -- adding $0.0044/bottle. Once that amortized cost is folded in (D5), The Guarding Upgrade's true total cost climbs to $0.028167/bottle -- 9.11% higher than The Rated Cap's $0.025600/bottle. A's case is real only if a Hero can show the contract volume is understated (case.json.sensitivity_disclosure) or argue the retrofit buys long-term flexibility beyond this one contract.
balance.argument_b: The Rated Cap requires no capital outlay, no dependency on the guarding contractor's single install slot clearing before the contract's first production week, and no risk that the retrofit is only partially justified if the contract runs shorter than expected. Its cost per bottle, $0.025600, is simply TC(150) -- fully computed, no assumption about future volume required. Once Appendix C's amortized retrofit cost is folded into The Guarding Upgrade's total (D5), The Rated Cap is the cheaper real path by 9.11%, even though the underlying calculus optimum (r*, D2) is not attainable under Line 3's current guarding at all.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |total_cost_per_bottle(Guarding Upgrade) - total_cost_per_bottle(Rated Cap)| / max(...), where total_cost_per_bottle(Upgrade) = TC(r*) + U/Q, total_cost_per_bottle(Cap) = TC(r_cap), TC(r) = CR(r)*MPU(r) = (a + b*r)*(1/r + d), r* = sqrt(a/(b*d)). a=$0.90/min (MA1/MA2, informed by [S1][S2]), b=$0.0004/(bottle/min) (MA3, informed by [S3]), d=0.02 min/bottle (MA4). r_cap=150 bpm (MA5, informed by [S4]). U=$44,000 (MA6, informed by [S5]), Q=10,000,000 bottles (MA7). r*=335.41 bpm, TC(r*)=$0.023767/bottle, TC(r_cap)=$0.025600/bottle, U/Q=$0.0044/bottle. total(A)=$0.028167/bottle, total(B)=$0.025600/bottle. margin=|0.028167-0.025600|/0.028167=9.11%, within the case's 8-15% target band and SPEC §2's 20% cap. Full arithmetic verified by sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Line 3's current rated maximum safe operating speed
modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: Line 3 is an older, conservatively-guarded machine within the industry's documented 100-500 bpm range [S4], not a new high-speed installation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's load-bearing, dilemma-flipping dial. Tier 2 P5 (±50% flex) found a -50% flex (150 -> 75 bpm) flips the verdict from The Rated Cap to The Guarding Upgrade (recomputed margin 9.14%, now favoring A) -- a more conservatively-guarded existing line makes the retrofit's amortized cost worth paying. +50% (150 -> 225 bpm) does not flip it (margin widens to 14.08%, still favoring B).

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source prices a full-line retrofit; [S5] prices a single interlocked door at $1,500-$5,000. This case's retrofit covers multiple hazard zones (turret access panels, infeed/outfeed conveyor guarding, an updated safety PLC), not one door -- $44,000 extends that per-door range to a comprehensive, multi-zone scope.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tier 2 P5 (±50% flex) found U does not flip the verdict either direction: +50% gives margin 15.70% (B still wins, and the margin is now wide -- see sensitivity_disclosure CAVEAT), -50% gives margin 1.41% (B still wins, but the two paths are nearly a tie).

modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: a multi-month exclusive co-packing commitment at realistic line utilization (well under running 24/7 at r*'s ~335 bpm for the full period).

Not dilemma-flipping, but disclosed as a CAVEAT (see sensitivity_disclosure): a materially smaller contract than assumed makes The Rated Cap's advantage larger than this case's own balance target, not smaller.

sensitivity_note: T4 tier requirement (SPEC §3): the case requires stating and defending at least one assumed quantity. Eight are stated (MA1-MA8); MA5 (Line 3's rated maximum safe speed) is the dilemma-flipping one -- see modeling_assumptions[MA5].sensitivity and sensitivity_disclosure below. MA7 (contract volume) does not flip the verdict but a -50% flex pushes the margin past SPEC §2's 20% cap -- disclosed as a CAVEAT, not an independent instability.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Line 3's own current rated maximum safe speed is protagonist-specific -- a fact about this particular machine's existing guarding, not independently verifiable from the general 100-500 bpm industry range [S4] alone. Tier 2 P5 found this dial flips the verdict from The Rated Cap to The Guarding Upgrade at -50% flex (75 bpm vs. the stated 150 bpm), because a more conservatively-guarded existing line makes the retrofit's amortized cost easier to justify. This is the case's single most load-bearing, dilemma-flipping assumption, consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA5].

Total contract volume on Line 3 is a forecast of a not-yet-fully-run commitment, not a measurable present fact. Tier 2 P5 found -50% flex (10,000,000 -> 5,000,000 bottles) does not flip the verdict (The Rated Cap still wins) but pushes the recomputed margin to 21.39% -- past SPEC §2's 20% cap. Disclosed as a CAVEAT rather than an independent instability: the direction of the finding (a smaller contract makes the safer, no-capital option look even better, not worse) is not surprising, but the resulting margin size is real and worth a human reading it as 'the gap widens further,' not as a literal, tightly-bounded percentage.
